These items imply fear of human attack rather than disaster-related threat.

Negative Appraisals: Institutional Failure could occur after a disaster, but in combination with the highly interpersonal Threat items it reinforces a different trauma narrative than natural disaster. The Memory items are disaster-compatible, but the Threat cluster is not clinically coherent with that trauma context.

The threat items are centered on anticipating intentional human intrusion or attack (planning escape routes, listening for someone entering the home), which is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma type of natural disaster. Heightened alertness to loud sounds could fit disaster trauma, but these two more specific threat beliefs imply a different trauma context.

The appraisal 'The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down' is possible after a disaster, but in this profile it pulls toward a betrayal/response-failure formulation that is not supported elsewhere by the selected threat or memory items. Combined with the intrusion-focused threat items, it weakens coherence with a natural-disaster trauma profile.

vignette:
# Marcus

Marcus was forty-five when the earthquake hit Haiti in 2010. He had been there for six weeks as a field medic with a volunteer surgical team, stationed in a converted school building in Port-au-Prince that served as a makeshift clinic. On the morning of January 12th, he was organizing supplies in the storage room—restocking bandages, checking expiration dates on medications—when the ground began to move. Not sway. Move. The concrete walls buckled inward with a sound he had never heard before and has never been able to describe to anyone since: a sound that seemed to come from the earth itself, a grinding, tearing shriek that made every cell in his body recognize danger at a frequency below thought.

He was buried for eighteen minutes. Not deeply—a partial collapse of the roof had created a pocket of space where he lay among fallen concrete and twisted rebar, his right leg pinned at the knee. The darkness was absolute. Around him, people were screaming, and above him, the sound continued—aftershocks, he would later understand, but in that moment it was the same apocalyptic noise, repeating, each time convincing him that the earth was opening further, that he was going deeper. He was extracted by other team members who dug with their hands. His leg was not broken, but the soft tissue damage was severe, and for three days he worked from a wheelchair, triaging injured people while his own body sang with pain and adrenaline.

When he returned to the States, Marcus expected to recover. He had training in trauma—he understood shock, understood the physiology of survival. But something in him had fundamentally reorganized. For months, he moved through his apartment in Arlington like a man clearing a minefield. Any unexpected sound—a car backfiring, a door slamming, the garbage truck's hydraulic hiss—sent him into a state of raw alertness that left him shaking and gasping. He had come to understand that the world was not what he had believed it to be. He had spent twenty-two years in the military, had trained to control environments, to save lives through precision and knowledge. The earthquake had taught him that control was an illusion, that the ground itself could betray you, that no amount of preparation mattered when the earth decided to move.

His wife, Patricia, had tried to help. She would find him in the dark at three in the morning, sitting in the kitchen with all the lights off, listening. When she asked him what he was listening for, he couldn't explain. He was listening for the sound. He was waiting for it to come again. She held him through nights when memories of the event would surface—not as coherent narratives but as fragments that refused to arrange themselves in order: the smell of dust, the weight of concrete on his chest, the face of a child he had pulled from rubble, the screaming that had no source. When these moments came, the terror that accompanied them was indistinguishable from the terror of the event itself. It was not memory; it was reliving. Patricia would hold him, and he would weep with a despair that frightened them both.

Patricia died of cancer four years later. Marcus had been at her bedside—he had known exactly what was happening, had watched her organs fail with the clinical precision of a medic—and yet he had been unable to prevent it, unable to fix it, unable to control the outcome. Her death compounded something that had been growing in him since Haiti: the conviction that nothing he did mattered, that meaning itself was a story people told themselves to feel safe, and that safety was a lie. He had stopped working as a medic two years before her death. He couldn't stand in a hospital. The sounds of monitors, the overhead pages, the fluorescent lights—all of it triggered a state of hypervigilance so overwhelming that he would have to leave.

Now, at forty-five, Marcus works as a contractor doing repairs and maintenance. He lives alone. He has not slept more than four hours in a night in fifteen years. He cannot attend social gatherings—the unpredictability of sound, of crowds, of other people's proximity makes it impossible. He has come to believe that he is no longer the person he was, that the version of himself who had faith in his abilities and meaning in his work has been erased. He has finally sought help not because he believes help is possible, but because his isolation has become absolute, and he is afraid of what he might do if it deepens any further.
